newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia race row MP linked to 'militant crazies'.
newsitem.headline: Australia race row MP linked to 'militant crazies'.

text.p: Senior Australian politicians including former foreign minister Gareth Evans said on Thursday that populist politician Pauline Hanson was linked to violent right-wing extremists.
Hanson, who campaigns against immigration, multiculturalism, Aboriginal welfare and a deeper Australian role in Asia, denies any links with right-wing militants.
But influential government figure Ron Boswell and Evans, now deputy leader of the Labor opposition, said the Queenslander had ties with groups urging violent and racist policies.
"There is no doubt that she is linked with the militant crazy right and they with her," Evans told reporters.

Boswell told the Senate on Wednesday night that Hanson's increasingly popular One Nation Party was linked to the League of Rights, militant gun groups that advocated violence against tougher gun laws, and other extremist factions.

"The facts are that Pauline Hanson's One Nation not only harbours and promotes extremists as office-bearers and potential candidates, but One Nation advertises in the anti-Semitic, racist and extremist rag, The Strategy," he said.
"As with all populist movements, the great majority of supporters have no idea of the hidden agenda of some of the key people.
"While she provides a temporary emotional outlet for fear and uncertainty, her solutions would only entrench trauma, insecurity and division."

Prime Minister John Howard, criticised for failing to act swiftly and firmly enough when Hanson sparked a divisive race row last year, told government backbenchers this week he would denounce her as an extremist with limited popular support in a key speech on Monday during an official visit to Britain.
He arrived in London on Wednesday to be greeted by criticism in leading British newspapers over his handling of race issues.
Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron, smarting at the British attack, defended Australia on Thursday as the world's least racist country.
"Australia is the most racially tolerant nation on earth," Herron said in a radio interview.

Australian church, union, human rights and community groups have published full-page advertisements in London papers urging Prime Minister Tony Blair and Queen Elizabeth, who is also Australian head of state, to press Howard over race and Australia's treatment of indigenous Aborigines.

Howard is under fire at home for refusing to apologise for an official policy that continued up to 1970 to take Aboriginal children from their families and for his planned solution to a land rights row between Aborigines and graziers.
Leading British broadsheets ran articles this week criticising the conservative leader.

"Mr Howard is struggling against widespread criticism of his handling of Aboriginal affairs, dissatisfaction from the business community over a stalled economy, and concern that he has failed to control the spreading racial debate driven by the maverick independent politician Pauline Hanson," the Daily Telegraph said.
Hanson has struck a chord with voters disillusioned by the major parties and worried by stubbornly high unemployment, a manufacturing recession and sluggish economic growth.
Opinion polls show One Nation has up to 10 percent support, enough to make it the third power in Australian politics if that is maintained to the next election, due by mid-1999.
